title: Family accuses police of using excess force
article: A mentally-ill man who died after police subdued him with pepper spray did not speak English well and may have been afraid of uniformed officers.
Relatives of Kasim Cakmak, 37, say they should have been notified before staff of the Alberta mental health board tried to have him committed to hospital.
"I think excessive force was used," said Nurbin Ciplak, Kasim's sister.
"He would be alive today had they called us. The way he died is too bizarre and too tragic."
Kasim, who suffered from schizophrenia, died Friday afternoon after two police officers and a nurse attempted to overpower him.

Police spokesperson Annette Bidniak said Friday that Kasim was increasingly aggressive with staff members at the mental health board's community living program downtown. When police arrived to help bring him to Alberta Hospital, he flew into "a violent rage," Bidniak said.

Pepper spray did not subdue him, so the officers and a male nurse wrestled him to the ground and handcuffed him. They noticed he had stopped breathing and tried cardiopulmonary resuscitation, but he was pronounced dead at the hospital.
Nurbin Ciplak said board staff had three phone numbers for the family, but no one bothered to inform them they were transferring her brother to Alberta Hospital.
"We have caller ID on the phone and they never called us," she said. "We were home all afternoon."

Kasim, a happy-go-lucky man who loved to play with his nieces and nephews at the park, had attended the community living program at 99th Avenue and 108th Street three times a week for the past two years to socialize with other patients, Nurbin said.
He liked it so much he got ready to go long before the bus arrived to pick him up.
"He liked to go and smoke, drink coffee and eat," she said. "He goes there to socialize and play bingo. It was not a treatment place. It's like a recreation place."
Kasim was on medication for his illness. He didn't need daily treatment and saw a psychiatrist every three months, she said.

She said the family wonders whether anyone bothered to tell police her brother was hard to communicate with because of his illness and a language barrier. He immigrated from Turkey in 1990, about eight years after the rest of the family.
Staff should have known Kasim might react unpredictably when he saw uniformed police officers coming at him, especially if he didn't understand what they wanted to do with him, she said.
"They should have phoned someone who speaks his language first."
The family didn't know Kasim had died until 6:30 p.m. when detectives showed up at another sister's house. They found out he was pepper-sprayed on the late-night news.
Nurbin said her 62-year-old mother blames herself for Kasim's death.
"She believes he wouldn't have died if she had been with him. She believes she could have done differently," Nurbin said, as her mother sobbed quietly beside her.

Kasim's death is even harder for his mother to accept because she is not allowed to see his body until Monday after an autopsy has been performed, Nurbin said. "She wants to see him before they cut him up."
Charles Vermeeren, spokesperson for the Alberta Mental Health Board, said Kasim's death was regrettable. It is normal for staff to call police if they have difficulty with a patient, he added.
Family friend Ray Turkhan said Kasim's death is completely senseless and should never have happened. He blames miscommunication rather than deliberate wrongdoing.
"I don't see it as him being berserk and violent," Turkhan said. "I see it has him being scared and panicking. This person feared for his life."
